Patients Served and Client Encounters, 2025

Row Psychiatric Services: from raw Tebra exports to final numbers

Kelly Adu-Gyamfi, Healthcare Data Analyst

October 21, 2026

The short answer

This report answers two simple questions about 2025:

  1. How many children, teens and adults did we serve in 2025? We served 1,804 people in total: 314 children (ages 5 to 13), 239 teens (ages 14 to 17) and 1,250 adults (18 and older). Each person is counted once, no matter how many times they came in. One additional patient was under 5 and is reported separately.

  2. How many patient encounters (visits) did we have in 2025? We had 19,283 encounters. An encounter is each time a patient came in and was seen by a provider. On average, each person was seen about 11 times during the year.

314
Children served (ages 5 to 13)
239
Teens served (ages 14 to 17)
1,250
Adults served (18 and older)
19,283
Client encounters (visits) in 2025

In 2025 Row Psychiatric Services saw 1,804 unique patients across 19,283 completed visits, an average of 10.7 visits per patient. About seven in ten patients were adults, and roughly three in ten were children or teens. One additional patient was under 5 at their first visit and sits outside the three requested groups; I report that patient separately so the totals still add up.

The rest of this report explains how I got there: what the raw data looked like, what I had to fix, the decisions behind each number, and what I think the numbers are telling us.

1 What I was asked, and how I defined it

Before counting anything I wrote down exactly what each term would mean. Most disagreements about numbers come from people quietly using different definitions, so I wanted these settled up front.

tibble::tribble(
  ~Term, ~`How I defined it`,
  "Encounter (visit)", "An appointment whose final status in Tebra is Checked Out. Cancelled, No Show, Rescheduled, and appointments that were never closed out do not count.",
  "Patient served", "A unique person with at least one encounter in 2025.",
  "Unique person", "Last name + first name + date of birth. The export has no MRN, so this is the most reliable key available.",
  "Children", "Ages 5 to 13",
  "Teens", "Ages 14 to 17",
  "Adults", "Ages 18 and older",
  "Which age to use", "Each patient is counted once, using their age at their first 2025 visit. That way a teen who turns 18 in July is not counted twice."
) |> nice_table(align = c("l", "l"))
Term How I defined it
Encounter (visit) An appointment whose final status in Tebra is Checked Out. Cancelled, No Show, Rescheduled, and appointments that were never closed out do not count.
Patient served A unique person with at least one encounter in 2025.
Unique person Last name + first name + date of birth. The export has no MRN, so this is the most reliable key available.
Children Ages 5 to 13
Teens Ages 14 to 17
Adults Ages 18 and older
Which age to use Each patient is counted once, using their age at their first 2025 visit. That way a teen who turns 18 in July is not counted twice.

2 How I got from raw exports to final numbers

I split the work into three separate R programs on purpose. Each one does one job, and none of them reaches into another’s job. This keeps the work auditable: anyone can see what the raw data looked like before I touched it, what I changed, and how the final numbers were calculated.

tibble::tribble(
  ~Step, ~Program, ~`What it does`, ~`What it does NOT do`,
  "1. Profile", "row_2025_appointments_profile.R", "Reads the 12 monthly exports exactly as they are and reports missing data, duplicates, inconsistent values and monthly patterns.", "Change, remove or recode anything.",
  "2. Clean", "clean_appointments_2025.R", "Applies documented cleaning rules and logs every row removed. Produces one analysis-ready file.", "Count patients or encounters.",
  "3. Analyze", "row_2025_patients_served_analysis.R", "Answers the questions, checks that every total reconciles, and produces tables and charts.", "Alter the cleaned data."
) |> nice_table(align = c("l", "l", "l", "l"))
Step Program What it does What it does NOT do
  1. Profile
row_2025_appointments_profile.R Reads the 12 monthly exports exactly as they are and reports missing data, duplicates, inconsistent values and monthly patterns. Change, remove or recode anything.
  1. Clean
clean_appointments_2025.R Applies documented cleaning rules and logs every row removed. Produces one analysis-ready file. Count patients or encounters.
  1. Analyze
row_2025_patients_served_analysis.R Answers the questions, checks that every total reconciles, and produces tables and charts. Alter the cleaned data.

2.1 Step 1: Getting to know the raw data

I loaded 12 monthly Tebra appointment exports (January through December 2025), giving 25,821 raw rows. Before deciding anything, I wanted to understand what a “row” actually was, what was missing, and whether anything would cause a person or a visit to be counted twice.

2.1.1 What is missing

show_png(profile_dir, "plot_missing")

A few things stood out:

  • Home phone is missing on about 88% of rows. That is not a problem for this report; most patients simply give a mobile number.
  • Patient name and date of birth are missing together on about 12.4% of rows. When I looked at those rows, they were not visits at all. They are provider schedule blocks and holds (time reserved on a calendar with no patient attached). This mattered: if I had counted every row, I would have inflated visits.
  • Provider is missing on a small but growing share of rows. The monthly view below shows it rising from well under 1% early in the year to about 4% by December. It does not affect these counts, but it is worth flagging to the front desk because it will matter for provider productivity reporting.
show_png(profile_dir, "plot_ready_missing_by_month")

2.1.2 Volume and appointment outcomes by month

show_png(profile_dir, "plot_month_volume")

Monthly volume was steady at roughly 1,650 to 2,150 patient rows, with the large majority Checked Out every month. The status mix is where the story gets more interesting:

show_png(profile_dir, "plot_month_status")

  • No-shows climbed in the last quarter, from around 5 to 7% for most of the year to over 9% in December.
  • Cancellations peaked in the summer (June and August), which fits with vacations and school breaks for our younger patients.
  • A small share of past appointments were never closed out in Tebra every month (still showing Ready To Be Seen, Confirmed or Scheduled). These are a data hygiene issue rather than a clinical one, and I come back to them in the decisions section.

2.1.3 Who comes in, and when

show_png(profile_dir, "plot_age_histogram")

The age distribution was the first hint at the final answer. There is a large peak among school-age children and young teens (roughly 8 to 18), then a long, gradual tail through adulthood into the 80s. Row is clearly serving a lot of families, not just adults.

show_png(profile_dir, "plot_weekday_hour")

Most appointments start between 9:00 and 16:00, with the busiest single slots mid-afternoon on Wednesdays and Tuesdays. Evening slots (17:00 onward) exist only Tuesday through Thursday. I noticed the after-school hours (15:00 and 16:00) are among the busiest, which again lines up with a large pediatric population.

2.1.4 Would anyone be counted twice?

show_png(profile_dir, "plot_ready_rows_per_patient")

Most patients have a handful of appointments in the year, but a long tail have 30, 50 or more. Those are patients in high-frequency services (IOP, TMS, ABA) and they are real, not duplicates. I did find three things that could double count people or visits if I were careless:

if (!is.null(dups)) {
  nice_table(dups |> mutate(rows = fmt(rows)),
             caption = "Duplicate checks from the profiling program",
             align = c("l", "r"))
} else cat("<p><em>duplicates_summary.csv not found in the profile folder.</em></p>")
Duplicate checks from the profiling program
check rows
Exact duplicate rows (every column identical) 0
Appt ID repeated (expected for recurring series) 727
Appt ID + date and time repeated (true duplicate key) 0
Same patient, same date and time, same provider (possible double entry) 9
Same patient, same date and time, different providers (possible double booking) 5
Same patient with more than one appointment on the same day 158
Same Appt ID + date appearing in more than one file (overlapping exports) 0
  1. Appointment ID is not unique. Recurring series reuse the same ID on different dates, so I could not use it alone to identify a visit.
  2. Names are typed inconsistently. The same person can appear as “SMITH, JANE”, “Smith , Jane” or “SMITH, JANE ANN”. Capitalization and spacing alone created 1 extra patient keys.
  3. Dates of birth carry a hidden time stamp (mostly 15:00) from a time zone shift in the export. Left alone, this pushes some birthdays to the wrong day and can change a patient’s age group. It changed the calculated age on 0 rows.

The profiling step ended with a list of decisions the cleaning program needed to make. None of the raw data was changed at this point.

2.2 Step 2: Cleaning the data

The cleaning program turned those findings into explicit, logged rules. Every row removed is accounted for.

if (!is.null(clog)) {
  nice_table(clog |> mutate(across(c(rows_removed, rows_left), fmt)),
             caption = "Cleaning log: rows removed at each step",
             align = c("l", "r", "r"))
} else cat("<p><em>cleaning_log_2025.csv not found.</em></p>")
Cleaning log: rows removed at each step
step rows_removed rows_left
Raw rows read 0 25,821
Removed: no patient name (provider blocks) 3,199 22,622
Removed: patient has no DOB 0 22,622
Removed: appointment outside 2025 0 22,622
Removed: DOB after visit date or before 1900 0 22,622
Removed: duplicate booking (same patient/provider/date-time) 9 22,613

What each rule does, in plain terms:

  • Dropped rows with no patient name (3,199 rows). These are provider schedule blocks, not visits.
  • Dropped rows with a patient but no date of birth (0 rows). Without a birth date I cannot place the person in an age group.
  • Kept only appointments dated in 2025.
  • Removed impossible birth dates (after the visit date or before 1900).
  • Removed true duplicate bookings: the same patient, same provider, same date and time. Where a duplicate existed, I kept the Checked Out copy so a real visit was never lost (9 rows).
  • Standardized names (uppercase, consistent spacing around commas) and fixed birth dates by rounding off the hidden time stamp.
  • Built a patient key from last name, first name and birth date, ignoring middle names so “DOE, JANE” and “DOE, JANE MARIE” are one person.
  • Calculated age two ways: age on the day of each visit, and age at the patient’s first completed visit of the year.

The result was one analysis-ready file of 22,613 appointments for 2025, with built-in checks that stop the program if any patient is missing a name, birth date or valid age.

2.3 Step 3: Counting and checking

The analysis program reads the cleaned file, checks it again (dates all in 2025, encounter flag matches Checked Out status, no duplicate encounters), and then counts. Before it writes anything, it confirms that:

  • the age groups add up to the total number of unique patients,
  • encounters by age group add up to total encounters,
  • encounters by month add up to total encounters.

If any of these fail, the program stops rather than producing a number that does not reconcile. All checks passed.

3 Results

3.1 Question 1: Children, teens and adults served

by_group |>
  transmute(`Age group`,
            `Patients served`        = fmt(patients_served),
            `% of patients`          = pct(pct_of_patients),
            `Encounters`             = fmt(encounters),
            `% of encounters`        = pct(pct_of_encounters),
            `Visits per patient`     = encounters_per_patient) |>
  nice_table(caption = "Unique patients served in 2025, by age at first visit",
             align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r")) |>
  row_spec(nrow(by_group), bold = TRUE, background = "#f3f7fd")
Unique patients served in 2025, by age at first visit
Age group Patients served % of patients Encounters % of encounters Visits per patient
Under 5 1 0.1% 14 0.1% 14.0
Children (5-13) 314 17.4% 3,889 20.2% 12.4

show_png(figures_dir, "01_patients_by_age_group")

1,250 adults, 239 teens and 314 children were served in 2025. Together, children and teens make up 30.6% of everyone Row saw. The single patient under 5 is shown separately because they fall outside the agreed groups.

3.1.1 Who uses the most visits?

show_png(figures_dir, "02_share_patients_vs_encounters")

show_png(figures_dir, "03_encounters_per_patient")

This was the finding I found most interesting. Children use more than their share of visits (17.4% of patients but 20.2% of encounters, averaging 12.4 visits each). Teens use noticeably fewer (13.2% of patients, 9.5% of encounters, only 7.6 visits each). Adults sit right at the clinic average.

I cannot say from appointment data alone why teens average fewer visits. It could be the services they are referred to, school schedules, or teens disengaging from care. It is a question worth raising with the clinical team, because adolescent engagement is something we can act on.

3.2 Questions 2 and 3: Encounters in 2025

year_sum |> nice_table(caption = "2025 at a glance", align = c("l", "r"))
2025 at a glance

There were 19,283 client encounters in 2025. Because the year is complete, “visits for the year so far” and “patient encounters in 2025” are the same number.

show_png(figures_dir, "04_encounters_by_month")

Visits were steady across the year, averaging about 1,607 a month. The low months (February and November) are mostly a calendar effect. February is short, and November had Veterans Day and Thanksgiving. Adjusting for the number of business days makes this clearer:

holidays_2025 <- as.Date(c("2025-01-01", "2025-01-20", "2025-02-17", "2025-05-26",
                           "2025-06-19", "2025-07-04", "2025-09-01", "2025-10-13",
                           "2025-11-11", "2025-11-27", "2025-12-25"))
days <- seq(as.Date("2025-01-01"), as.Date("2025-12-31"), by = "day")
bdays <- data.frame(Month = month.abb[as.integer(format(days, "%m"))],
                    wk = as.integer(format(days, "%u")), d = days) |>
  filter(wk <= 5, !d %in% holidays_2025) |>
  count(Month, name = "business_days")

by_month |>
  left_join(bdays, by = "Month") |>
  mutate(Month = factor(Month, levels = month.abb)) |>
  arrange(Month) |>
  transmute(Month,
            Encounters               = fmt(encounters),
            `Running total`          = fmt(cumulative_encounters),
            `Business days`          = business_days,
            `Encounters per business day` = round(encounters / business_days, 1)) |>
  nice_table(caption = "Encounters by month, with a per-business-day rate",
             align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))

3.2.1 How many scheduled appointments became visits?

show_png(figures_dir, "05_appointment_outcomes")

Of 22,613 appointments scheduled in 2025, 85.3% became completed visits. The rest were no-shows (1,515), cancellations (1,435), reschedules, and 278 past appointments that were never closed out in Tebra.

4 Decisions and caveats leadership should know about

1. “Ready To Be Seen” appointments are not counted. There are 252 appointments where the patient was marked as arrived but the visit was never checked out. I left them out to stay conservative, but in the October 2026 billing worklist most Ready To Be Seen appointments had in fact been billed. If leadership agrees these were real visits, the 2025 total becomes 19,535. I recommend we confirm a sample against billing before deciding.

2. One patient was under 5. The agreed groups start at age 5, so this patient (14 visits) is reported separately rather than folded into Children.

3. Age is taken at the first visit of the year. 66 patients had a birthday during 2025 that moved them into a different age group. Counting them by first-visit age means each person is counted exactly once. If we instead group each visit by age on that day, adults account for 13,679 encounters instead of 13,553. The total does not change either way.

4. There is no MRN in the export. Patients are identified by name and birth date. I standardized names and ignored middle names, but two different spellings of the same person (for example a typo in the last name) could still be counted as two people. The profiling program flags possible spelling variants by birth date so they can be reviewed in Tebra. Adding the MRN or Tebra patient ID to the export would remove this risk entirely.

5 What I would do next

  • Close out stale appointments. Work with the front desk on the 278 past appointments still sitting open, and agree whether Ready To Be Seen should count as a visit going forward.
  • Add the patient ID to the Tebra export. This is the single biggest improvement to accuracy for every future count.
  • Look at teen engagement. Pair the teen visit pattern with visit reasons and referral sources to understand whether this is expected or a retention gap.
  • Watch the rising no-show rate. The late 2025 increase deserves a closer look by provider and visit type.
  • Make this repeatable. The three programs can be rerun on 2026 data with only the year changed, so this report can become a quarterly update.
